title: Praise
hook: hands raised, songs repeated, worship loud and joyful

segments.voice: Yesterday, the love feast: plain bread, water, and testimony. Your line was bread and a story. Who did you eat with, and what story did you tell? Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

The ark of God is coming up into Jerusalem, with shouting and the sound of the trumpet, and the king can't keep still. "And David danced before the LORD with all his might." His wife Michal watches from a window and despises him for it. A king, leaping in the street. David's answer: he'll be lowlier still in his own eyes, before the LORD who chose him. A new week, and a new room: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, whose worship can look a lot like David in the street. Today's word: praise.

Step into a Pentecostal or charismatic service and you may find a band, a congregation on its feet, hands in the air, one chorus sung again and again, someone calling out amen, someone in tears, someone very still. From the back row it can look like a concert. To the people there, it's praise: thanking God out loud, with the whole body. Much of it has old roots. Raised hands appear in scripture. Psalm 134 says, "Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD." And Paul's first letter to Timothy pictures people praying everywhere, "lifting up holy hands." Open hands, held up, the way a child reaches for a parent. The repeated songs have old roots too. Psalm 136 gives a reason to thank God, and every verse ends with the same answer: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Again and again, until the line isn't something you think about but something you stand on. The word hallelujah comes from the psalms too. Psalm 150 ends, in the King James, "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD." That last phrase, in Hebrew, is hallelujah. Christians praise at very different volumes. Orthodox chant, a quiet Anglican evensong, the silence of a Quaker meeting, a Pentecostal church on its feet. The psalms make room for all of them. The same book that says "Be still, and know that I am God" also says, "O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph."

Here's the practice, and it may feel unusual; that's all right. Let your breath settle. If you're somewhere you can, lift your hands, palms open, to shoulder height or higher, and hold them there for a few slow breaths. Notice what your body does with that. Then lower them slowly to your lap, and rest. If you pray, you can say the last line of the psalms: Praise ye the LORD. If you don't, simply let your open hands be a kind of thank-you for one good thing today. The bell holds the time.
Praise. Thanking God out loud, with songs, raised hands and the whole body. In Hebrew, hallelujah.
Your line: hands up. Today, when something good happens, even something small, lift your hands for a second, in private if you'd rather. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

howItsDone: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, worship often includes a band, raised hands, repeated choruses and spoken praise; other churches praise through chant, hymns or silence.

fork.setup: you're David. you've danced before the LORD in the street, and your wife says it was beneath a king. what do you say?
options: she's right; it won't happen again.
I'll be lowlier still, before the LORD who chose me.
fork.reveal: David doesn't apologize. he says he'll be even lowlier in his own eyes, because the dancing was before the LORD.

original.note: Hebrew: hallelujah. at the end of Psalm 150 the King James renders it praise ye the LORD.

trapdoor: what you thought: praise means loud music and hype.
what it means: thanking God with the whole self, voice, hands and feet, loud or quiet.
what a scholar hears: where the King James ends Psalm 150 with praise ye the LORD, the Hebrew says hallelujah; the psalms ask for both stillness and shouting.
recall: a psalm in rhyme and steady meter
